name: Armenian Catholic Church — Újbuda
description: The Armenian Catholic church at Orlay utca 6 in Szentimreváros serves Budapest's Hungarian-Armenian Catholic community and is dedicated to Our Lady of Ransom and Saint Gregory the Illuminator. It grew out of a villa bought in the 1960s, and the parish centre was renovated with state support in 2022.

children.text: The Armenian Catholic church stands at Orlay utca 6 in Szentimreváros, in Budapest's 11th district, Újbuda. Its Hungarian name is Fogolykiváltó Boldogasszony és Világosító Szent Gergely-templom, and it is dedicated to Our Lady of Ransom and Saint Gregory the Illuminator. It follows the Armenian rite and belongs to the Archdiocese of Esztergom-Budapest, according to GCatholic. Wikimedia Commons describes it as one wing of the parish building rather than a freestanding church.

A study published by the Budapest City Archives explains how the community came to be here. Most of the Armenians living in Budapest descend from the Hungarian-Armenian community of Transylvania. After the First World War and the Treaty of Trianon, many Hungarian Armenians moved to Hungary, and the community sought its own church and its own priest. For a very long time Roman Catholic churches in Budapest hosted the Armenian Catholic community.

The Orlay utca site came later. According to the same study, in the 1960s the Mechitarist priest Dániel Kádár gave up his family's properties and collected donations among Armenians in Hungary and Western Europe. With the money he bought a villa on Orlay utca, where a pastoral office, a chapel, a museum and a library were set up. The study quotes a community member who said that people went to the Orlay utca chapel as if to their first family.

In November 2022 the renovated Armenian parish centre was inaugurated. The National Catholic Register reported that Cardinal Péter Erdő and the Armenian Catholic Patriarch Raphaël Bedros XXI Minassian blessed it, that the Hungarian government funded the work through the Hungary Helps Program, and that the centre is to host educational and cultural projects and the archives of the Hungarian-Armenian community.
Good to know
This is a working Armenian Catholic parish, not a conventional sightseeing stop. Check access and service times with the parish before visiting.
Orlay utca is in Szentimreváros in the 11th district, so it fits a visit to that part of Újbuda.
The Budapest City Archives study shows a wrought-iron gate on Orlay utca, but do not assume the chapel or the parish centre is open to visitors.

historyIntro: The Armenian Catholic church on Orlay utca grew out of a villa bought in the 1960s for Budapest's Hungarian-Armenian Catholics. Its history is tied to the Transylvanian Armenians who settled in the capital in the twentieth century.

historySections.heading: A community that settled in Budapest

children.text: According to a study by the Budapest City Archives, most of the Armenians living in Budapest descend from the Hungarian-Armenian community of Transylvania. They arrived in a first wave among the civil servants of the period after 1850, and in a second wave after the First World War and the Treaty of Trianon, when many Hungarian Armenians who had lost their livelihoods moved to Hungary. The community then wanted its own church and its own priest. For a very long time, however, different Roman Catholic churches in Budapest hosted the Armenian Catholic community.

The same study says that in the 1960s the Armenian Catholic Mechitarist priest Dániel Kádár started a fundraising effort, giving up his family's properties and collecting donations among Armenians in Hungary and in Western Europe. He succeeded in buying a villa on Orlay utca, where an Armenian Catholic pastoral office, a chapel, a museum and a library were set up. Interviews in the study describe the Orlay utca chapel as a place where people felt at home, as if it were their first family.

In November 2022 the renovated Armenian parish centre in Budapest was inaugurated. The National Catholic Register reported that Cardinal Péter Erdő and the Armenian Catholic Patriarch Raphaël Bedros XXI Minassian blessed the premises and that the Hungarian government paid for the renovation through the Hungary Helps Program. The renovated section is intended to host educational and cultural projects and the archives of the Hungarian-Armenian community.

name: Pozsonyi Road Reformed Church
description: The Pozsonyi úti Reformed Church, known as the Hálaadás or Thanksgiving church, stands at Pozsonyi út 58 in Újlipótváros. Built between 1936 and 1940 to designs by Imre Tóth and Jenő Halászy, it has a classical portico, a separate tower and Bauhaus-influenced interiors, and its basement once sheltered people in hiding.

children.text: The Pozsonyi úti Reformed Church stands at Pozsonyi út 58 in Újlipótváros, in Budapest's 13th district, between Pozsonyi út, Garam utca, Gogol utca and the Újpesti rakpart. The parish describes the site as just north of Margaret Bridge, facing Margaret Island. It is a Reformed, or Calvinist, church, known as the Hálaadás temploma, the Church of Thanksgiving.

The congregation began in a first meeting house on Tutaj utca, consecrated in 1926, and outgrew it. The Reformed Church received the new plot from the municipality; it was marshy ground that had to be taken into account in the building. A design competition was announced in 1935. Imre Tóth won first place and Jenő Halászy second, and both took part in the construction. Work began on 6 December 1936 with a thanksgiving service on the empty plot, and the foundation stone was laid on 25 April 1937.

Sources describe the design in different words. WeLoveBudapest calls the church neoclassical, with Bauhaus features in the interior and the ancillary buildings, unusual aisle windows, a separate bell tower and Greek-style columns. The parish describes a classical building with a full-width portico, a central cross and a tall separate tower. Hungarian Wikipedia lists the style as Bauhaus. Construction took about four years, with stoppages caused by money shortages and the approaching war. Sulfurous water surfaced from the ground, which forced a redesign, and the tower was built on pile foundations. The church was consecrated on 8 December 1940.

The church was badly damaged in 1944, when it stood between German artillery fire from Buda and Soviet fire from Pest. The Danube-side entrance, part of the colonnade and the organ were hit, and damage marks remained visible until the building was restored in 1972. During the later war years the basement sheltered deserters, resistance members and mainly Jewish families, and pastor Albert Bereczky, who had led the construction, was recognised as Righteous Among the Nations.

Today the church is used for services, religious classes and Bible lessons, and WeLoveBudapest reports a basement theatre hall seating more than two hundred people. Hungarian Wikipedia says the crypt, with a stage and event hall, is rented out for various events.
Good to know
The parish website shows a liturgical calendar but no visiting hours, so check access and service times with the parish before going.
The church faces Margaret Island and stands just north of Margaret Bridge, which makes it easy to combine with a walk by the Danube.
The basement theatre hosts performances, so ask the parish whether anything is on during your visit.

historyIntro: The Pozsonyi úti Reformed Church was built between 1936 and 1940 for a congregation that had outgrown its first meeting house. Its history includes severe war damage in 1944 and a rescue effort in its basement.

historySections.heading: From Tutaj utca to a design competition

children.text: The Reformed congregation first met at the corner of Tutaj utca and Visegrádi utca, and the parish website says its first permanent meeting house on Tutaj utca was consecrated in 1926. It outgrew that site and received a new plot from the municipality, on marshy ground. A design competition was announced in 1935. Imre Tóth won first place and Jenő Halászy second, and both took part in the construction. Lajos Simkovics, a civil engineer, supervised the works.

Work began on 6 December 1936 with a thanksgiving service on the empty plot, and the foundation stone was laid on 25 April 1937, with Bishop László Ravasz recorded by the parish as laying it. The ground was raised with soil and more than three hundred piles were driven. Construction took about four years because of stoppages caused by the approaching war, shortages of money and sulfurous water that surfaced from the ground, which forced a redesign, especially of the tower, which stands on pile foundations. The church was consecrated on 8 December 1940, before the Second World War broke out.

The church came through most of the war largely unscathed but was severely damaged in 1944, standing between German artillery fire from Buda and Soviet fire from Pest. The Danube-side entrance, part of the colonnade and the organ were hit, and damage marks remained visible until 1972, when the building was restored. After the war the basement served as a warehouse for about fifty years and was later returned to use as a theatre. Parish information says repairs were completed by 1972, and a destroyed facade pillar was restored for the church's fiftieth anniversary.

stories.title: Hiding in the basement

children.text: WeLoveBudapest reports that during the later war years the basement of the church sheltered deserters, wanted resistance members and mainly Jewish families who had false papers. Pastor Albert Bereczky, who had led the church's construction, and members of his congregation were involved.

According to the article, the basement had its own toilet, so those hiding did not need to come up, they received food, and a child was born there. No one was discovered by the Germans, the Arrow Cross or the Soviets. Bereczky received the Righteous Among the Nations award.

name: Rumbach Street Synagogue
description: Rumbach Street Synagogue, designed by Otto Wagner and consecrated in 1872, is an octagonal Moorish Revival synagogue in the Jewish Quarter of Erzsébetváros. After decades of decay it was restored and reopened in 2021, and, according to its official site, it is still a synagogue that also hosts concerts and events and serves as an exhibition space of the Jewish Museum and Archives.

children.text: Rumbach Street Synagogue stands at Rumbach Sebestyén utca 11–13 in Erzsébetváros, in the area of the former Pest ghetto. Hungarian Wikipedia gives it a second name, the Little Synagogue, to tell it apart from the Dohány Street Synagogue. It was built for traditionalist Jews of the Status Quo Ante community, the congregation formed around the 1869 schism in Hungarian Jewry, although the building's official site says the Neolog community commissioned it with fittings suited to traditional liturgy. The Center for Jewish Art records Otto Wagner, then an emerging Viennese architect, as its designer.

Sources give slightly different dates for the start of construction: English Wikipedia says 1869, and Hungarian Wikipedia says 1 May 1870. The work was paid for by public donations. The prayer space was consecrated on 1 October 1872, and the use permit followed in May 1873. The building is of brick, in a neo-Moorish style, and the prayer hall has an octagonal plan.

The facade is symmetrical. Its two octagonal side sections are said to represent the biblical pillars Jachin and Boaz, and, according to Hungarian Wikipedia, they are topped with lotus-flower carvings and continue in small domed towers that resemble minarets. Sources describe the colours of the restored facade differently, so the exact palette is left unstated here; according to Hungarian Wikipedia, its central part carries the two tablets of Moses. Inside, an octagonal dome rests on eight slender iron columns with Alhambra-style capitals, and the walls carry gold, blue and red reliefs. English Wikipedia calls the design an homage to the Dome of the Rock in Jerusalem, though not an exact copy.

The building's later history was hard. In 1941 Jews were gathered in it before being deported to Kamianets-Podilskyi, and a plaque commemorates them. Worship ended in 1959, the roof over the Torah ark collapsed in 1979, the building was evacuated in 1980 and it was looted in 1982. After years of state ownership it passed to the Mazsihisz Jewish federation in 2005, and works began in 2017. The König-Wagner architects' office led the restoration, using Wagner's surviving plans and historic photographs, and the building was officially reopened on 10 June 2021.

The building's official site says it is still a synagogue, that it also hosts concerts, lectures and events, and that it serves as an external exhibition space of the Jewish Museum and Archives; the Center for Jewish Art likewise records that in 2021 it was open to the public as a synagogue, museum and concert hall. Hungarian Wikipedia adds that it can still be used for ritual purposes and also hosts concerts, cultural events and conferences, and that a hydraulic mechanism in the middle of the octagon can raise or lower the Torah reading platform. Modern chairs have replaced the original wooden benches.
Good to know
Visiting arrangements depend on its mix of uses as a synagogue, museum and event venue, so check the current official information for opening times and tickets before you go.
It is also a synagogue, so ask the organisers what applies on the day of your visit.
Under the dome, look for the eight slender iron columns with their Alhambra-style capitals and the gold, blue and red reliefs.

historyIntro: Rumbach Street Synagogue was built for the Status Quo Ante community in the early 1870s and then spent decades in decay before a restoration that ended in 2021. Its history follows the changing fortunes of Jewish Pest.

historySections.heading: Building for the Status Quo Ante, 1869 to 1873

children.text: English Wikipedia says the building was begun in 1869, during the schism in Hungarian Jewry, and Hungarian Wikipedia gives the start of construction as 1 May 1870, with the Jewish congregation applying for the building permit only on 14 June 1870. Otto Wagner designed the synagogue, and the work was funded by public donations. The prayer space was consecrated on 1 October 1872, and the use permit was issued on 10 May 1873. It was intended for traditionalist Jews who found the Neolog synagogues too liberal.

In 1941 Jews were gathered in the building before Hungarian authorities deported them to Kamianets-Podilskyi in occupied Ukraine, where Germans murdered them. A plaque commemorates them. During the Second World War only the residential part of the building suffered minor damage. After 1956 about eighty congregants remained, and the synagogue was no longer used for worship from 1959. In 1979 the roof above the Torah ark collapsed, and the women's gallery later collapsed as well. The building was declared life-threatening and evacuated in 1980, and unknown perpetrators looted it in 1982.

In the 1980s a state construction company bought the building from the congregation, and in the 1990s preservation work restored the sanctuary but left the renovation unfinished. The Mazsihisz Jewish federation received the building in 2005, and from 2006 it was open to visitors without its interior fittings. Works began in 2017, designed by the König-Wagner office on the basis of Wagner's surviving plans and historic photographs, and the Hungarian ICOMOS committee gave the restoration an award in 2019. The renovated building was officially opened on 10 June 2021.
